# Getting Started with R {#sec-getting-started-with-r}

*(Source materials: DataCamp, Hands-On Programming with R, swirl — see [Resources](resources.qmd).)*

Chapters 1–8 all assume you can already run R code and read what it prints back — they
teach data analysis *with* R, not R itself. If you have never written a line of R before,
start here rather than at [Chapter 1](01-understanding-data.qmd). If you already know a
little R or another programming language, skim this page and move on to [Rubric
10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd) or straight to [Chapter
1](01-understanding-data.qmd).

## Installing R

**R** is a free, open-source language and environment for statistical computing. Download
it from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/), the official R repository, and pick the
installer for your operating system. Accept the default options during installation.
Install R first — [Rubric 10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd) covers **RStudio**, the
friendlier interface this module's instructions assume you're using, which needs R
already installed to run.

## Learning the Basics

Rather than duplicating a full introduction to R here, this module points you to
**[DataCamp's "Data Analyst with R" career track](https://app.datacamp.com/learn/career-tracks/data-analyst-with-r)**,
an interactive, browser-based course that teaches R hands-on, no prior programming
experience assumed. The early "Introduction to R" course is enough to follow Chapters
1–4; you don't need to complete the whole track before moving on.

::: {.differentiation-box}
::: {.struggling}
If reading someone else's R code still feels like reading a foreign language:
[swirl](https://swirlstats.com/students.html)'s "R Programming" module is a good
companion to DataCamp — short, interactive exercises that run directly in your own R
console.
:::
::: {.deeper}
If you'd rather work from a short, structured book than an interactive course:
[Hands-On Programming with R](https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/) starts from
absolute zero and builds toward writing your own small functions and simulations.
:::
:::
